# The Van That Almost Burned Down (And What I Wish I'd Checked)

Last Wednesday, October 28th, I was in a client's driveway in Bedford drying Moose, a very fluffy Bernese, on high. My inverter was running the dryer and I was pretty much on autopilot. I smelled hot plastic and assumed it was the dryer motor, because that's what I'd been listening to all afternoon and that's what I expected to smell. Then I saw smoke coming up out of the bench seat where my batteries live.

I killed the battery switch, grabbed the extinguisher, and got Moose out the side door still damp. He was thrilled about it, honestly. I was not.

Everyone's okay. Moose is fine, his people are fine, I'm fine. The van isn't. I'm off the road for at least three weeks while the parts come in, and I've had to cancel 31 appointments so far, which is its own kind of gut punch when you're a mobile groomer and your whole income is that van. Rent is due on the 1st. I'm trying not to think about that too hard.

I'm writing this up properly for two reasons. The first is that I need to get it out of my head. The second is that a few of you read this blog because you're groomers too, some of you are in the same position of buying or building a mobile setup, and one of you, Tasha, is about to put a deposit down with the same person who built mine. So this one's for you, Tasha, and for anyone else who has a van, a trailer, or a box of batteries they're trusting with a lot of power.

Before anything else: **I am not an electrician.** I'm a dog groomer who now knows way more about 12-volt wiring than she ever wanted to. Everything in here about the electrical side is what I learned from Priya at Sackville Marine Electric, who came out to look at the damage and walked me through it. If you take one thing from this post, let it be this: get a qualified person to look at your system. I'll say that again at the end, because it matters.

## The setup

The van was built in spring 2025 by Coastline Van Fitouts. Darren did the build. I'd like to be clear that the build looked great. It was clean, tidy, the cabinetry was nice, the wiring was neatly routed and tucked away. That's part of why I trusted it. You don't go looking for problems in something that looks that good.

The power system was:

- A 3000W inverter
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries, 12V
- A 300A ANL fuse
- The cable running from the battery to the inverter, which was 4 AWG

The dryer I use pulls somewhere around 1800 to 2000 watts. Add the water heater sometimes, and I was looking at a load that, at 12 volts, works out to somewhere in the range of 150 to 250 amps running through that cable. That's the number I didn't really understand until after the fire, and it's the number that matters most.

## What went wrong

Priya laid it out for me in a way I could follow, and I'm going to try to pass it along the same way. There were a few separate problems, and they stacked on top of each other.

**1. The cable was too small.**

According to Priya, a 3000W inverter running off 12 volts should have had 2/0 cable between the battery and the inverter. I had 4 AWG. At 12 volts, a lot of current is going through that wire, and the thinner the wire, the more it resists that current and the more heat it makes. Her point was that the cable wasn't built for the load it was carrying, so it was running hot all the time I was using the dryer. It wasn't a sudden failure. It was a slow one.

**2. The positive lug was crimped badly.**

The lug is the metal end piece that clamps onto the cable and bolts to the battery or inverter. On the positive end of my cable, the crimp had been done with something like pliers or a hammer, not a proper hydraulic crimper. A good crimp compresses the lug and the cable strands into one solid connection. A bad one leaves gaps, and gaps mean the connection has higher resistance, and higher resistance means more heat right at the connection point.

What made it worse was the heat-shrink. Somebody had put heat-shrink over the crimp, which looked neat and finished, but it was hiding the problem. Nobody could see what was happening underneath it, including me.

**3. The fuse was too far from the battery.**

The 300A ANL fuse was mounted about 90cm away from the battery. Priya said it should be within about 18cm, which is roughly 7 inches. The reason is that the section of cable between the battery and the fuse is the part that's unprotected if something goes wrong. If there's a short in that stretch, the fuse isn't going to stop the current flowing through it. The closer the fuse is to the battery, the less unprotected cable there is.

So the fuse was doing its job for the stretch of cable closest to the inverter, but the long section near the battery had no protection at all.

**4. There was no smoke detector in the back.**

The only smoke detector was the one that came with the van, up in the cab. Nothing in the living area and nothing near the batteries. I didn't know I should have had one there, and honestly I'm not sure the build would have included one even if I'd asked. I'm adding one now. More on that later.

## What the damage looked like

When Priya pulled up my photos, the positive lug was black. The heat-shrink had melted back about 3cm from the crimp, and the cable jacket had melted back too. Under that, the copper was discoloured. That's the kind of thing you don't see unless you're looking for it, and it's exactly what you'd expect from a connection that was running hot for a while.

Here's the part that really got to me. Priya brought up thermal camera shots of her own van running a similar load, and her setup barely gets warm. Her wiring was sized right, her connections were done properly, her fuse was where it needed to be. Next to hers, mine looked like a different system entirely. The difference was wild, and it was all stuff that would have been invisible if you'd just looked at the van from the outside.

## What I'd tell you to check on your own setup

I'm going to give you the checklist I wish I'd had. Do all of this with the power off, the battery disconnected, and the van completely de-energized. If you're not comfortable with any step, stop and call someone who is.

**Battery to inverter cable**

- Check the cable gauge against what the inverter manufacturer or your installer recommends for that inverter's wattage and voltage. Don't assume thicker-looking is the same as right. Ask for the number in writing.
- Look along the whole length for melted or cracked jacket, especially near the battery and near the inverter, and anywhere the cable bends sharply or rubs against metal.
- Check that the cable isn't sitting against anything hot or anything that could chafe through.

**Lugs and crimps**

- Look at every lug on both ends. Are they crimped with a proper crimping tool? A hydraulic crimper is the standard for this kind of cable. If you can't tell, ask.
- Look for discolouration. Black, brown, or blue lugs or cable ends are a red flag.
- Gently tug each cable at the lug. It shouldn't move at all. If it wiggles, the crimp is not solid.
- Be suspicious of heat-shrink that's covering a crimp. You want to be able to see the crimp. If it's hidden, ask the installer to show you what's underneath.

**Fuses**

- Find your main fuse. Is it within about 18cm (7 inches) of the positive battery terminal? If it's far away, that's a problem worth raising.
- Check the fuse rating against the cable and the load. A 300A fuse on a cable that can't handle 300A is not protecting the cable. The fuse is supposed to blow before the wire does.
- Make sure the fuse holder is secure and not hot.

**Battery switch and connections**

- Check the battery switch for discolouration or heat marks.
- Check the battery terminals and bolts. They should be tight and clean, with no green or white corrosion building up.

**Smoke and fire safety**

- Do you have a smoke detector anywhere close to the batteries and the back of the van, not just in the cab? If not, add one. A heat or smoke alarm near the power system is cheap and it's the thing that would have woken me up if I'd been inside.
- Have a fire extinguisher that's rated for electrical fires, and know where it is. Make sure you can reach it from the driver's seat without climbing over things.
- Keep a clear path to the side or rear door.

**Using an infrared thermometer after a big load**

This is where the $40 Canadian Tire thermometer comes in. After you've been running a big load for a while, say 30 minutes or so, go back and check the temperatures:

- Lugs at both ends of the battery cable
- The inverter cable where it runs along its length
- The fuse and fuse holder
- The battery switch
- The battery terminals

Compare each reading to the ambient temperature around the van and to the other connections. Anything noticeably warmer than the rest is worth investigating. It doesn't have to be dramatic. If you can't keep your hand on it comfortably, it's too hot.

One thing to know about infrared thermometers: they read surface temperature, and shiny metal can read lower than it really is. So a lug might look cooler on the thermometer than it actually is. That's why you compare readings across connections and track changes over time, rather than trusting one number. If something looks suspiciously cool in a spot where you'd expect heat, that's not a reason to relax. Check it again, and get it looked at.

Also, a thermometer is a warning tool, not a safety system. It can tell you something's getting hot. It can't stop it from getting hot.

## What I'm asking the groomer girls to do

Tasha, especially, but really everyone: if you're buying a van, a trailer, or a build of any kind, before you pay a deposit, ask the builder for the following **in writing**:

- The cable gauge for every power run, and what it's rated for
- The fuse ratings and the location of each fuse
- The inverter model and its wattage
- The battery specs
- Who did the crimps, and what tool they used
- Whether there's a smoke or heat alarm near the power system

If they push back on putting it in writing, or if they seem annoyed that you asked, that tells you something too. A good builder should be happy to answer these questions, because they're the questions that matter most.

And ask whether the system has been checked by a qualified electrician, not just the person who built it. Ask whether they can show you thermal or load-test results. Ask what the warranty covers and what it doesn't.

Tidy is not the same as right. I trusted my build because it looked good. I'm not going to make that mistake again, and I'd rather you didn't either.

## I'm not an electrician, get a pro to look

I keep coming back to this, but it's the most important thing in the whole post. I learned everything in this post from Priya, who is qualified, and from a bad afternoon in a driveway. I'm not in a position to tell you whether your specific system is safe. Only someone who can physically look at your wiring, your connections, and your load can do that.

If you have any doubt at all about your setup, have a qualified marine or RV electrician or a certified auto electrician look at it. It's worth the money. It's worth it even if you think everything is fine.

## Where I'm at

As of today, the van is still in the shop. The parts are on order and the repair is quoted at $4,200, which covers rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block, and a class T fuse. The shop is saying three weeks minimum, and that's the minimum, not the estimate. I'm hoping that's accurate.

Insurance has said "maybe" on coverage so far. The adjuster is coming Thursday, and I'm holding my breath about that. I'll update when I know what they decide.

Darren hasn't responded to my three texts or the email I sent. I'm not writing this to go after him publicly. I'm writing the facts I know, because people deserve to have them when they make their own decisions. I'll leave it to readers to decide what to make of it. If that changes, or if I have anything to add, I'll say so here.

As for me, I'm honestly scared. I keep replaying the moment I smelled that plastic and thinking about how it could have gone differently. Moose's mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her steps while I shook, and I don't think I'll ever forget that. Some people show up in the worst moments in a way that really matters.

I'm also making plans. I'm adding a heat alarm near the batteries. I'm getting an infrared thermometer, which I already have, and I'm going to use it. I'm going to find a way to keep my clients through this, even if it means rescheduling and taking a hit on income. And I'm going to figure out rent.

I'll post again when the van's back on the road, and I'll tell you how it went.

In the meantime: check your cables, ask for the specs in writing, and don't let anyone hide a crimp under heat-shrink from you.

Stay safe, and go hug your dogs.
